Persuasion
per-SWAY-zhun
n. (the act of persuading; a settled conviction or belief produced by argument or influence)
Latin persuasio, from persuadere, to persuade fully, from per-, thoroughly, and suadere, to advise or urge. A persuasion is a conviction that has been thoroughly worked into a man, whether by truth or by flattery.

Biblical Definition

Paul's letter to the Galatians uses the word at the exact hinge of his argument against the false teachers who had persuaded a once-faithful church to add circumcision to the gospel of grace. Having asked Ye did run well; who did hinder you that ye should not obey the truth?, he delivers a verdict on the persuasion itself, wherever its precise human source lay: This persuasion cometh not of him that calleth you. The word here does not name error in the abstract; it names a specific, successful campaign of conviction that had genuinely taken hold in the Galatian churches, strong enough to turn them from a course they had begun well.

What makes Paul's verdict sharp is its indifference to how convincing the persuasion felt from the inside. He does not argue that the Galatians were stupid or that the false teachers were unpersuasive; he grants, if anything, that the persuasion had worked. His whole point is that a persuasion's actual origin, not its felt plausibility or its emotional force, is what determines its worth: this persuasion, however thoroughly it had been worked into them, did not come from the one who called them by grace, and its true source, not its psychological grip, is therefore what the Galatians must judge it by.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): the act of persuading; the state of being persuaded; a settled opinion or conviction produced by argument or entreaty.

expand to see more

PERSUASION, n. The act of influencing the mind by argument, entreaty, or reason; also, a fixed opinion or belief resulting from such influence.

HINDER, v.t. To obstruct; to impede; to prevent from progress or accomplishment.

GRACE, n. The free and unmerited favor of God; the divine influence operating in the heart for salvation.

GOSPEL, n. The good news of salvation through Jesus Christ; the doctrine of Christ's redemptive work.

CALL, v.t. To invite or summon; in theology, to invite effectually to salvation through the gospel.

Key Scripture

Gal 5:7 — "Ye did run well; who did hinder you that ye should not obey the truth?"

Gal 5:8 — "This persuasion cometh not of him that calleth you."

Gal 1:6 — "I marvel that ye are so soon removed from him that called you into the grace of Christ unto another gospel:"

Gal 1:8 — "But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed."

Modern Corruption

A persuasion's felt sincerity or emotional force is treated as evidence of its truth, when Paul's whole argument concedes the Galatians were genuinely, successfully persuaded and still condemns the persuasion outright on the basis of its actual source.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; persuasion still names a settled conviction produced by influence. The principle worth recovering is exactly what Paul's verdict refuses to grant: that a persuasion which has genuinely taken hold, changed real behavior, and felt entirely convincing from the inside might, for that very reason, be trustworthy.

Galatians one supplies the standard by which every persuasion, however effective, must actually be judged — not by its psychological grip but by whether it comes from him that calleth, the God of grace, or from another gospel dressed up convincingly enough to run alongside the true one. Paul's willingness to pronounce a curse on even an angel preaching a different gospel shows how completely the source, not the felt strength, of a persuasion determines its worth in his theology.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek peismone (G3988), a persuasion, a yielding to persuasion; the noun of Galatians 5:8, used only here in the New Testament, from peitho, to persuade.

expand to see more

Greek peismone (G3988) — a persuasion, a state of having been persuaded; a rare noun, used only at Galatians 5:8 in the whole New Testament.

Greek peitho (G3982) — to persuade, to win over, to convince; the verb root behind peismone.

Greek enkopto (G1465) — to hinder, to impede, literally to cut into a path; the verb behind “hinder” in Galatians 5:7.

Greek kaleo (G2564) — to call, to invite; the participle behind “him that calleth you,” the true source Paul contrasts with the false persuasion.

Greek anathema (G331) — a thing accursed, set apart for destruction; the fate Paul pronounces on any persuasion preaching another gospel, Galatians 1:8.

Usage

"“This persuasion cometh not of him that calleth you” — Paul's verdict on the Galatians' false conviction."

"“Ye did run well; who did hinder you” — the question the persuasion is measured against."

"“so soon removed from him that called you into the grace of Christ” — the true source that persuasion had displaced."
